Studies on Pretreatment Strategies and Bacterial Consortia for the Accelerated Biodegradation of Microplastics

Abstract:

The widespread accumulation of synthetic polymers, particularly low-density polyethylene (LDPE), generated by industrial packaging and consumer use pollutes terrestrial and aquatic environments, creating severe ecological hazards. One of the most common recalcitrant microplastics present in diverse ecosystems is LDPE. Due to its high molecular weight, three-dimensional cross-linked backbone, and pronounced hydrophobicity, LDPE is chemically inert, resists natural weathering, and persists for centuries. To protect ecological integrity and aquatic life, microplastics must be effectively eliminated from contaminated environments and wastewater streams. Microorganisms can be harnessed to biologically depolymerize these recalcitrant plastics into non-hazardous metabolic byproducts through sustainable bioremediation.

The present study focuses on the isolation, screening, and characterization of potent polymer-degrading bacterial strains from municipal dumpsite environments and the formulation of an optimized bacterial consortium to enhance degradation kinetics. To overcome the high activation energy barrier and surface inertness of microplastics, pretreatment methods are evaluated to introduce reactive functional groups and improve bacterial attachment. This study also includes the design, fabrication, and operation of a two-chamber reactor system to assess the scalability and practical application of the process for wastewater treatment.

In the initial study, 42 bacterial isolates obtained after multi-cycle enrichment in Mineral Salt Medium containing PEG 8000 were screened via clear zone assays, identifying active strains with clearance ratios greater than 1.3. Evaluation of selected isolates in a 30-day degradation assay with commercial LDPE demonstrated that Strain 6211 and Strain 622 achieved gravimetric weight reductions of 3.69% and 3.34%, respectively, significantly higher than the abiotic control. The structural and surface alterations of the degraded polymer were confirmed through ATR-FTIR spectroscopy, Raman spectroscopy, X-ray diffraction, and Environmental Scanning Electron Microscopy, validating active chemical oxidation, decreased relative crystallinity, and microbial surface colonization.
